items.title: Deep Learning, Transformers & Neural Networks: How Modern AI Learns
items.summary: Modern AI did not come from traditional programming. It came from a series of architectural breakthroughs, and three terms trace the whole path. Terms covered: - Neural Networks: layers of interconnected nodes that adjust millions of connections based on the errors they make, learning from examples rather than following instructions - Deep Learning: stacking many layers so each level learns more abstract representations. Early layers detect edges and tones, middle layers find shapes, later layers recognize complex concepts. - Transformer: the 2017 architecture that introduced attention, weighing the relevance of every part of an input against every other part at once. Every major language model today is built on it. From a single connected node, to the power of depth, to the attention mechanism that made language AI possible. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #DeepLearning #NeuralNetworks #Transformers #AIGlossary #H2Oai

items.title: Building AI Benchmarks with Zapier, ARC Prize, and Ramp (Panel)
items.summary: At Bench Summit 2026 in San Francisco, a panel of AI benchmark builders discussed what it takes to create and maintain benchmarks that stay useful as models improve. Lukas Bergstrom, Lead PM for AI Evals and Benchmarks at Zapier, moderates a conversation with Robin Salimans, Principal Engineer, Applied AI at Zapier, Greg Kamradt, President of ARC Prize, and Shaiyon Hariri, Senior Research Engineer at Ramp. What the panel covers: * Whether benchmarks will still matter in two to three years * How building benchmarks is changing as models saturate them faster * Measuring hard-to-verify skills like creativity, hypothesis testing, and clear communication * Public versus internal evals, and how much to share without shortening a benchmark’s life * What the panelists found most surprising about building benchmarks * Why reading traces matters * Audience Q&A Chapters: 0:00 Welcome and AutomationBench 1.5 0:30 Will benchmarks still matter in two to three years? 1:02 How building benchmarks is changing 3:12 Why unsaturated benchmarks are getting harder to build 3:40 Verifying creative and abstract tasks 5:10 Can a model design the benchmark for its successor? 5:46 How Ramp approaches benchmarks 9:16 Where AutomationBench 2 is headed 11:42 Measuring hard-to-verify skills and verifiable domains 13:38 Squaring benchmarks with company strategy 14:52 The most surprising things about building benchmarks 18:39 Testing ARC tasks with real people 19:37 What makes a benchmark successful 22:07 Internal hill climbing versus public benchmarks 25:26 Why reading traces matters 27:43 Audience QA

items.title: Evaluating the Frontier with Google DeepMind’s Gemini Team (Panel)
items.summary: At Bench Summit 2026 in San Francisco, Google DeepMind’s Logan Kilpatrick moderates “Evaluating the Frontier,” a panel on how the Gemini team evaluates its models and works with the benchmark ecosystem. The panel features Kate Olszewska, who works on model release evals; Tao Jiang, who leads model quality evals for post-training; and Eric Deng, who works on evaluation for verticals like finance and legal. items.summary: Kate Olszewska, Product Manager at Google DeepMind, takes the stage at Bench Summit 2026 in San Francisco to share what’s new in Gemini 4 Carbon. items.title: If AI Makes Everyone Qualified, Who Gets Hired?
items.summary: Free weekly newsletter on how to win in an AI Disrupted world. Subscribe to the AI Survival Guide: https://ai-survivalguide.com/ 🐤My Twitter - https://twitter.com/KenJee_DS 👔 LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/in/kenjee/ AI can make all 244 applicants for a job look perfect on paper. What may decide who gets hired is a number scientists keep finding: about 150. In this video I follow Matt, who lost his marketing job after eleven years and couldn't get one human to write back. I look at why his big network didn't help, using Robin Dunbar's research on how many relationships one brain can keep track of. Then I bring in Safi Bahcall's idea about why companies change as they grow, and why both land near the same number. In Ashby's look at 38 million applications, referred people got an interview about 40% of the time, compared with about 3% for people who applied on their own. I'm also fair about the limits, since 150 is an average and that debate is still going. I use AI every day, but it can't be the person who vouches for you. I also share how I'm building small groups on purpose, plus a ten-minute exercise for tonight. Which of your rings feels thinnest right now: your 5, your 15 or your 50? items.title: Chips Are Being Built Like Skyscrapers

This clip delves into the atomic-level accuracy needed for processes like atomic layer deposition to create chips with hundreds of layers.
